A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InverseCrafter and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Shared content can be reliably matched despite extensive reformatting and additional material in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original camera-control and video-editing experiments in Tables 1–2, mask and guidance ablations in Figures 7–8, and appendix runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for unseen camera trajectories, alternative solvers and another video-model backbone in Appendix E.

M1.justification: Equation (5) revises the stated mask-training target from h=f(...) to h=1-f(...), changing the defined target for the learned encoder. The encoder architecture, L1-plus-SSIM objective and DDS/CG pipeline remain. The training-free alternative is retained in Appendix D, not removed.

E1.justification: VidSTG training, UltraVideo camera control and DAVIS text-guided editing remain. v2 additionally evaluates camera control on a DAVIS subset with unseen trajectories (Appendix E.5, Table 5), extending coverage to a focused generalization scenario.

E2.justification: v2 adds CogNVS to the main camera-control comparison in Table 1 and Figure 5. It also adds elementwise division as a mask comparator and displays interpolation, FlowDPS, FlowChef and PSLD solver variants in Figure 12. The existing main baselines and editing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 changes the recommended alpha from 0.6 to 0.8 and revises the tested alpha values; the runtime table is relabeled accordingly. Added ablations use CogVideoX and alternative solver configurations, while the reconstruction comparison drops MSE reporting. Main training budgets, resolutions and benchmark metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's mask-resizing, pixel-space DDS and alpha analyses, v2 tests elementwise mask division, compatibility with several inverse solvers, transfer to CogVideoX and generalization to unseen trajectories (Table 3, Figure 12 and Table 5). These substantially expand the questions experimentally examined.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. Both use point estimates and qualitative examples.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the learned model's PSNR/FVD of 28.95/102.46 with 29.35/99.73 alongside the revised alpha setting, and removes the original UltraVideo training-free row. Reconstruction results also change: learned-mask PSNR is 31.02 in v1 Figure 7(a) versus 27.97 in v2 Table 3, where binary resizing now has the highest SSIM. These are revised reports, not established same-setting gains or losses. CogNVS and Appendix E add substantial new results; Table 2's editing scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (5) changes the mathematical mask definition to the complement of the normalized latent difference. Appendix D's proxy formula retains the uncomplemented form, without reconciling that convention. The DDS objective and background diffusion/flow mathematics remain; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central latent-space inpainting and low-overhead claims remain. v2 explicitly frames the contribution as establishing operator equivalence, makes the learned encoder primary, and qualifies the training claim as requiring no VDM fine-tuning or annotated 4D training data.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly acknowledges that applying the target-view mask to the source video does not create a physically valid observation, and explains the localization and moderate-semantic-change assumptions supporting this fallback. The conclusion adds failure conditions involving large viewpoint changes, insufficient visible context and heuristic mask-target normalization. These substantially clarify applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicit code-availability statement and project-repository link, reducing access information without establishing that the code became unavailable. Most architecture, optimizer, training-budget and hardware details remain, while the documented alpha setting changes to 0.8.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including CogNVS, FlowChef, hard-data-consistency inverse solving and dynamic view synthesis as an inverse problem. Section 2.2 and Appendix C extend the existing comparison with SILO through arguments about supervision, varying masks and one-time operator prediction. The broader research positioning remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and preliminaries are extensively rewritten around target-view recapture and operator equivalence. Method subsections become explicit, CG pseudocode moves into the main text, and the training-free discussion moves into an expanded Appendix D alongside a new SILO discussion.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the paper into a single-column layout, redraws Figures 2–3, adds runtime-quality plots to Figure 1 and introduces process and solver-comparison figures. The former Figure 7 is reorganized into Table 3 and a redrawn alpha plot, and Table 5 adds a combined evaluation display. Most appendix qualitative examples are retained and resized.

improvement.justification: The added solver, backbone and unseen-trajectory tests broaden empirical support beyond v1's main benchmarks. Appendix D and the expanded limitations also make the method's assumptions easier to assess. These gains are tempered by incomplete specifications for the new evaluations, the unreconciled mask-complement convention and removal of the project code link. Overall quality improves modestly through stronger validation and qualification, independently of the revised performance scores.
